sections.heading: Session management
sections.prose:
After [installing the SDK](/quickstart#installation), authenticate with the username and password for your OpenProtein.AI account. [`openprotein.connect()`](/references/python-api/openprotein#openprotein.connect) looks up each credential in this order:

1. **Function arguments:** `username` and `password` passed to `openprotein.connect()`.
2. **Environment variables:** `OPENPROTEIN_USERNAME` and `OPENPROTEIN_PASSWORD` set in the environment where you run Python.
3. **Configuration file:** `~/.openprotein/config.toml` in your home directory.

Use environment variables or a configuration file to keep credentials out of scripts and notebooks. To use a configuration file, create the `.openprotein` folder in your home directory and save this as `config.toml`, replacing the placeholders with your credentials:

```toml
username = "your_username"
password = "your_password"
```

The file stores your password in plain text. Keep it private and out of version control.

Once you've set the environment variables or created the file, connect without passing credentials:

```python
import openprotein

session = openprotein.connect()
```

If authentication fails, check your credentials and whether environment variables are overriding the file. Use the `session` to [run your first model](/references/python-api/models#interface).

Create an authorized session with `openprotein.connect`, then use `session.models` to discover and run models. The session also exposes compatibility interfaces and other platform services, including clustering.

sections.heading: Referenced types
sections.prose: Types referenced by the interfaces above.
These data primitives represent a unified interface to working with our platform, whether it be structure prediction, binder design or inverse folding.

sections.heading: Protein
sections.prose: [`Protein`](#openprotein.molecules.Protein) is a fundamental primitive for working with proteins on the platform. These can be uploaded to our platform as a [`Query`](#openprotein.prompt.Query) to be used with models like [`ProteinMPNN`](#openprotein.models.ProteinMPNN) or [`ESMIF1`](#openprotein.models.ESMIF1) (e.g. for inverse-folding), as well as for ease of reuse. Construct a chain with `Protein(sequence)` and attach an MSA or templates with its properties or setters before folding. Use the mask methods to describe masked sequence or structure positions.

sections.heading: Complex
sections.prose:
[`Complex`](#openprotein.molecules.Complex) describes a molecular complex representation. These can be uploaded to our platform as a [`Query`](#openprotein.prompt.Query) to be used with models like [`RFdiffusion`](#openprotein.models.RFdiffusion), (e.g. for multi-chain binder design) as well as for easy reuse. Inspect chains with `get_chains()` or `get_chain()` and build or update them with `insert_chain()` and `set_chain()`.

Construct a complex from chain IDs and molecule objects:

```python
from openprotein.molecules import Complex, Ligand, Protein

complex = Complex({"A": Protein("ACDEFGHIK"), "B": Ligand(ccd="ATP")})
proteins = complex.get_proteins()
```

sections.heading: Structure
sections.prose: [`Structure`](#openprotein.molecules.Structure) describes a collection of [`Complex`](#openprotein.molecules.Complex) instances. These are typically created when parsing structure files (e.g., CIF, PDB) that contain multiple models of the same molecular complex, such as NMR ensembles or computational predictions with multiple conformations.

sections.heading: Ligand
sections.prose:
[`Ligand`](#openprotein.molecules.Ligand) represents a ligand that can be described either by ``smiles`` or ``ccd``. These are intended to be used as part of a [`Complex`](#openprotein.molecules.Complex).

Provide exactly one of `ccd` or `smiles`; providing both or neither raises `ValueError`.

sections.heading: DNA
sections.prose:
[`DNA`](#openprotein.molecules.DNA) represents a DNA chain. These are intended to be used as part of a [`Complex`](#openprotein.molecules.Complex).

DNA sequences accept A, C, G and T (case-insensitive); other letters raise `ValueError`.

sections.heading: RNA
sections.prose:
[`RNA`](#openprotein.molecules.RNA) represents a RNA chain. These are intended to be used as part of a [`Complex`](#openprotein.molecules.Complex).

RNA sequences accept A, C, G and U (case-insensitive); other letters raise `ValueError`.

sections.heading: Template
sections.prose: [`Template`](#openprotein.molecules.Template) describes a template that can be used for constraining fold jobs.

Upload your dataset to OpenProtein.AI's engineering platform for train, predict and design tasks. `session.data.Assay.create()` takes a pandas DataFrame with a `sequence` column. Measurement columns hold properties for training; identify free-text columns separately as metadata.

This example uses an [authenticated session](/references/python-api/openprotein#session).

```python
import pandas as pd

table = pd.DataFrame({
    "sequence": ["ACDE", "ACDF"],
    "activity": [1.2, 0.8],
    "notes": ["first", "second"],
})
assay = session.data.Assay.create(table, name="Example", metadata_columns=["notes"])
```

See the [assay upload guide](/how-tos/dataset/upload-assay) for more detail.

sections.heading: Alignments and sampled prompts
sections.prose:
[`session.data.MSA`](#openprotein.data.DataAPI.MSA) and [`session.data.Prompt`](#openprotein.data.DataAPI.Prompt) are resource classes bound to your session. Use `create()` to upload a file, `list(limit=...)` to browse your resources, and the class with `id=...` to load an existing resource. Omitting `limit` reads every page.

Start a homology search through [`session.align`](/references/python-api/align), load its stored MSA, and sample a prompt. You can submit sampling while the search is running. PoET accepts the prompt handle while sampling is still running.

```python
sequence = b"MKTAYIAKQRQISFVKSHFSRQLEERLGLIEVQAPILSRVGDGTQDNLSGAEK"
search = session.align.create_msa(sequence)
msa = session.data.MSA(id=search.id)
prompt = msa.sample_prompt(replicates=2, max_msa_sequences=10, seed=42)
job = session.models.poet.embed([sequence], prompt=prompt)
print(job.id)
```

`wait()` returns the ready handle. Index or iterate it to load its content. An MSA yields `(name, sequence)` pairs; a prompt yields one list of sequences per replicate. A failed or canceled job raises `JobFailedException` when you call `wait()` or `get()`. Uploaded resources are ready immediately and have no job ID.

```python
msa.wait(timeout=600)
print(msa[0])
for replicate in prompt.wait(timeout=600):
    print(replicate[:3])
```

**See also**

- Use [`session.align`](/references/python-api/align) to build an alignment. If you already have the file, [`session.data.MSA.create()`](#openprotein.data.MSA.create) replaces the deprecated [`session.align.upload_msa()`](/references/python-api/align#openprotein.align.AlignAPI.upload_msa).
- [`session.data.Prompt.create()`](#openprotein.data.Prompt.create) uploads prompt data as one FASTA file per replicate. Use [`session.prompt.create_prompt()`](/references/python-api/prompt#openprotein.prompt.PromptAPI.create_prompt) to build a prompt from Python sequences, `Protein` objects, or `Complex` objects.

examples.class:
msa = session.data.MSA(id="your-msa-id").wait(timeout=600)
print(msa.id, len(msa))
for name, sequence in msa[:3]:
    print(name, sequence)
examples.create:
from pathlib import Path

alignment = Path("alignment.a3m")
msa = session.data.MSA.create(
    alignment.read_bytes(), format="a3m", filename=alignment.name,
)
print(msa.id)
examples.list:
for msa in session.data.MSA.list(limit=5):
    print(msa.id, msa.name)
examples.sample_prompt:
prompt = msa.sample_prompt(replicates=2, max_msa_sequences=10, seed=42)
prompt.wait(timeout=600)
print(prompt[0][:3])

examples.create:
prompt = session.data.Prompt.create(
    [">first\nACDE\n", b">second\nACDF\n"],
    name="Two replicates",
)
print(prompt.id, prompt[0])
examples.list:
for prompt in session.data.Prompt.list(limit=5):
    print(prompt.id, prompt.name)
examples.update:
prompt.update(name="Reference prompt", description="Two FASTA replicates")
print(prompt.name, prompt.description)

sections.prose: Use `session.models` to run a model. If you know which model you want, use a named accessor such as `session.models.esm2`. To browse available system models, see [List models](#list-models). To look up a model by ID, call `session.models.get_model(model_id)`.

sections.heading: Interface
sections.prose:
With an [authenticated session](/references/python-api/openprotein#session), submit an embedding job and wait for its result:

```python
model = session.models.esm2
job = model.embed(["ACDEFGHIK"], reduction="MEAN")
embedding = job.wait(timeout=600)[0]
print(embedding.shape)  # (D,): one pooled NumPy vector
```

See [Task results](#task-results) for result types and [Jobs](/references/python-api/jobs) for reloading jobs and reading named outputs.

sections.heading: List models
sections.prose:
[`session.models.list_models()`](#openprotein.models.ModelsAPI.list_models) lists the system models available on the platform. By default it returns model IDs (`list[str]`). Set `verbose=True` for [model cards](#openprotein.models.ModelMetadata), which include display names and supported methods. Use `path` to filter by method; `path=["embeddings"]` matches models with an embedding method.

```python
model_ids = session.models.list_models()
print(model_ids[:5])

cards = session.models.list_models(verbose=True, path=["embeddings"])
for card in cards[:5]:
    print(card.model_id, card.name)
```

System model listings exclude your fitted models. Use [`session.models.GP.list()`](#openprotein.models.GP.list), [`session.models.SVD.list()`](#openprotein.models.SVD.list), or [`session.models.UMAP.list()`](#openprotein.models.UMAP.list) to list your fitted models by family. Since SDK 0.18.1, these methods return up to 100 fitted models by default and warn when a default call returns 100. Pass `limit=None` to read every page from `offset`, or set an explicit `limit` to cap the total. Set `offset` to skip results.

```python
fitted_gps = session.models.GP.list(limit=100)
print([gp.id for gp in fitted_gps])
if len(fitted_gps) == 100:
    next_gps = session.models.GP.list(limit=100, offset=100)
```

sections.heading: PoET-2
sections.prose:
OpenProtein-developed conditional and multi-modal protein language model that embeds, scores, and generates sequences conditioned on an input protein family.

*[Understanding protein function with a multimodal retrieval-augmented foundation model](https://www.doi.org/10.52202/085713-1772)* · [GitHub](https://github.com/OpenProteinAI/PoET-2)

The `PoET2` class below is the interface for `poet-2`. It supports sequence tasks and fitting downstream models.

| Model ID | Accessors | Interface |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `poet-2` | [`poet2`](#openprotein.models.ModelsAPI.poet2), [`poet_2`](#openprotein.models.ModelsAPI.poet_2) (alias of `poet2`) | [`PoET2`](#openprotein.models.PoET2) |

```python
from openprotein.molecules import Protein

model = session.models.poet2
msa = session.align.create_msa("MKTAYIAKQRQISFVKSHFSRQ")
prompt = msa.sample_prompt(num_sequences=10)
backbone = Protein.from_filepath("backbone.cif", chain_id="A")

job = model.embed(["MKTAYIAKQRQISFVKSHFSRQ"], reduction="MEAN", prompt=prompt)
embeddings = job.wait()
print(embeddings[0].shape)

job = model.logits(["MKTAYIAKQRQISFVKSHFSRQ"], prompt=prompt)
logits = job.wait()
print(logits[0].shape)

job = model.attn(["MKTAYIAKQRQISFVKSHFSRQ"], prompt=prompt)
attention = job.wait()
print(attention[0].shape)

job = model.score(["MKTAYIAKQRQISFVKSHFSRQ"], prompt=prompt)
log_likelihoods = job.wait()
print(log_likelihoods[0])

job = model.single_site("MKTAYIAKQRQISFVKSHFSRQ", prompt=prompt)
substitution_scores = job.wait()
print(substitution_scores[0])

job = model.indel("MKTAYIAKQRQISFVKSHFSRQ", insert="A", prompt=prompt)
indel_scores = job.wait()
print(indel_scores[0])

job = model.generate(prompt=prompt, query=backbone)
sequences = job.wait()
print(sequences[0])
```

sections.heading: Boltz-2
sections.prose:
Boltz-2 all-atom structure prediction model that jointly predicts complex structure and ligand binding affinity. Predicts protein, DNA, RNA and ligand complexes, with optional constraints, templates and experimental-method conditioning.

*[Boltz-2: Towards Accurate and Efficient Binding Affinity Prediction](https://www.doi.org/10.1101/2025.06.14.659707)* · [GitHub](https://github.com/jwohlwend/boltz)

| Model ID | Accessors | Interface |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `boltz-2` | [`boltz2`](#openprotein.models.ModelsAPI.boltz2) (alias of `boltz_2`), [`boltz_2`](#openprotein.models.ModelsAPI.boltz_2) | [`Boltz2`](#openprotein.models.Boltz2) |

```python
from openprotein.molecules import Protein

model = session.models.boltz2
protein = Protein("MKTAYIAKQRQISFVKSHFSRQ")
protein.msa = session.align.create_msa("MKTAYIAKQRQISFVKSHFSRQ")

job = model.fold(protein)
structure = job.wait()[0]
conformation = structure[0]
chain = next(iter(conformation.values()))
print(chain.sequence.decode())
print(chain.coordinates.shape)  # (L, 37, 3): residues, atom slots, xyz
```

sections.heading: RFdiffusion
sections.prose:
De novo protein backbone generation by diffusion.

*[De novo design of protein structure and function with RFdiffusion](https://www.doi.org/10.1038/s41586-023-06415-8)* · [GitHub](https://github.com/RosettaCommons/RFdiffusion)

The `RFdiffusion` class below accepts the supported design inputs. For legacy reloads, see [RFdiffusionFuture](#openprotein.models.RFdiffusionFuture).

| Model ID | Accessors | Interface |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `rfdiffusion` | [`rfdiffusion`](#openprotein.models.ModelsAPI.rfdiffusion) | [`RFdiffusion`](#openprotein.models.RFdiffusion) |

```python
from openprotein.molecules import Protein

model = session.models.rfdiffusion
query = Protein.from_expr(80)

job = model.generate(query=query)
design = job.wait()[0]
for chain_id, chain in design.items():
    if isinstance(chain, Protein):
        print(chain_id, chain.sequence.decode(), chain.coordinates.shape)
```

sections.heading: ESM2
sections.prose:
ESM2 masked protein language model trained on UniRef50. Its checkpoints share training data and objective, and differ in size.

650M parameters over 33 layers.

*[Evolutionary-scale prediction of atomic level protein structure with a language model](https://www.doi.org/10.1101/2022.07.20.500902)* · [GitHub](https://github.com/facebookresearch/esm)

**ESM2 (150M).** 150M parameters over 30 layers.

**ESM2 (35M).** 35M parameters over 12 layers.

**ESM2 (3B).** 3B parameters over 36 layers.

**ESM2 (8M).** 8M parameters over 6 layers.

| Model ID | Accessors | Interface |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `esm2_t33_650M_UR50D` | [`esm2`](#openprotein.models.ModelsAPI.esm2) (alias of `esm2_t33_650M_UR50D`), [`esm2_t33_650M_UR50D`](#openprotein.models.ModelsAPI.esm2_t33_650M_UR50D) | [`ESM2`](#openprotein.models.ESM2) |
| `esm2_t30_150M_UR50D` | [`esm2_t30_150M_UR50D`](#openprotein.models.ModelsAPI.esm2_t30_150M_UR50D) | [`ESM2`](#openprotein.models.ESM2) |
| `esm2_t12_35M_UR50D` | [`esm2_t12_35M_UR50D`](#openprotein.models.ModelsAPI.esm2_t12_35M_UR50D) | [`ESM2`](#openprotein.models.ESM2) |
| `esm2_t36_3B_UR50D` | [`esm2_t36_3B_UR50D`](#openprotein.models.ModelsAPI.esm2_t36_3B_UR50D) | [`ESM2`](#openprotein.models.ESM2) |
| `esm2_t6_8M_UR50D` | [`esm2_t6_8M_UR50D`](#openprotein.models.ModelsAPI.esm2_t6_8M_UR50D) | [`ESM2`](#openprotein.models.ESM2) |

```python
model = session.models.esm2

job = model.embed(["MKTAYIAKQRQISFVKSHFSRQ"], reduction=None)
embedding = job.wait()[0]
print(embedding.shape)  # (T, D): tokens (including special tokens), features

job = model.logits(["MKTAYIAKQRQISFVKSHFSRQ"])
logits = job.wait()
print(logits[0].shape)

job = model.attn(["MKTAYIAKQRQISFVKSHFSRQ"])
attention = job.wait()
print(attention[0].shape)

job = model.single_site("MKTAYIAKQRQISFVKSHFSRQ")
substitution_scores = job.wait()
print(substitution_scores[0])
```

sections.heading: ProteinMPNN
sections.prose:
Message-passing inverse-folding model that designs sequences for a fixed protein backbone.

The original weights, trained on protein structures from the PDB.

*[Robust deep learning-based protein sequence design using ProteinMPNN](https://www.doi.org/10.1126/science.add2187)* · [GitHub](https://github.com/dauparas/ProteinMPNN)

**SolubleMPNN.** Weights trained on soluble proteins only, for designing soluble sequences.

The `ProteinMPNN` class below is the interface for `proteinmpnn` and `solublempnn`, a checkpoint trained on soluble proteins. It generates and scores sequences.

| Model ID | Accessors | Interface |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `proteinmpnn` | [`proteinmpnn`](#openprotein.models.ModelsAPI.proteinmpnn) | [`ProteinMPNN`](#openprotein.models.ProteinMPNN) |
| `solublempnn` | [`solublempnn`](#openprotein.models.ModelsAPI.solublempnn) | [`ProteinMPNN`](#openprotein.models.ProteinMPNN) |

```python
from openprotein.molecules import Protein

model = session.models.proteinmpnn
query = Protein.from_filepath("backbone.cif", chain_id="A")

job = model.score([query.sequence], query=query)
log_likelihoods = job.wait()
print(log_likelihoods[0])

job = model.single_site(query.sequence, query=query)
substitution_scores = job.wait()
print(substitution_scores[0])

job = model.embed([query.sequence], query=query)
embeddings = job.wait()
print(embeddings[0].shape)

job = model.generate(query=query)
sequences = job.wait()
print(sequences[0])
```

sections.heading: ESMFold2
sections.prose:
ESMFold2 all-atom structure prediction model. Folds protein, DNA, RNA and ligand complexes.

Full-depth folding trunk (48 layers), optionally conditioned on an MSA.

*[Language Modeling Materializes a World Model of Protein Biology](https://www.doi.org/10.64898/2026.06.03.729735)* · [GitHub](https://github.com/Biohub/esm)

**ESMFold2-Fast.** Inference-optimized single-sequence variant (no MSA) whose folding trunk has half the depth (24 layers).

| Model ID | Accessors | Interface |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `esmfold2` | [`esmfold2`](#openprotein.models.ModelsAPI.esmfold2) | [`ESMFold2`](#openprotein.models.ESMFold2) |
| `esmfold2-fast` | [`esmfold2_fast`](#openprotein.models.ModelsAPI.esmfold2_fast) | [`ESMFold2`](#openprotein.models.ESMFold2) |

```python
from openprotein.molecules import Protein

model = session.models.esmfold2
protein = Protein("MKTAYIAKQRQISFVKSHFSRQ")
protein.msa = session.align.create_msa("MKTAYIAKQRQISFVKSHFSRQ")

job = model.fold(protein)
structure = job.wait()[0]
conformation = structure[0]
```

sections.heading: Task results
sections.prose:
Model methods return futures for their submitted tasks. See [how to read task results](/references/python-api/jobs#task-results) or [read a fitted model](/references/python-api/jobs#fitted-model-results).

For a specialized task future with per-position result type `T`, `get()` and `wait()` return `list[T]`. `get_item()` and unit reads return one `T`; `stream()` yields results in order. Bare reads select the task's primary output. Use `get(output=...)` or `wait(output=...)` to select a named output, which has its own result type.

sections.heading: Fitted models
sections.prose:
Use `session.models.SVD`, `session.models.UMAP` and `session.models.GP` to create estimators. Their fitting methods return fit futures. Call `get()` or `wait()` on the fit future to retrieve the fitted model, or select `output=...` to read a named fit output. See [fitted-model results](/references/python-api/jobs#fitted-model-results) for fit and cross-validation futures. Inspect the fitted model card for its advertised methods.

Replace `your-assay-id` with the ID of an existing [assay dataset](/references/python-api/data). All three estimators fit on the same embeddings job for the assay's sequences. Set `new_sequences` to the sequences you want to transform or predict on after fitting. For the UMAP example, use an assay with more than five distinct sequences.

```python
assay = session.data.Assay(id="your-assay-id")
embedding_job = session.models.esm2.embed(assay, reduction="MEAN")
new_sequences = ["ACDEFGHIK", "ACDEYGHIK"]
```

**SVD: project onto two components**

```python
svd_fit = session.models.SVD(n_components=2).fit(embedding_job)
svd = svd_fit.wait()
projections = svd.transform(new_sequences).wait()
print(projections[0].shape)
```

**UMAP: map sequences into two dimensions**

```python
umap_fit = session.models.UMAP(n_components=2, n_neighbors=5).fit(embedding_job)
umap = umap_fit.wait()
coordinates = umap.transform(new_sequences).wait()
print(coordinates[0].shape)  # (2,)
```

**GP: predict a measured property**

Replace `activity` with the name of a measurement column in the training assay that contains observed values.

```python
measurement = "activity"
gp_fit = session.models.GP(kernel="rbf").fit(embedding_job, property=measurement)
gp = gp_fit.wait()
predictions = gp.predict(new_sequences).wait()
first_prediction = predictions[0][measurement]
print(first_prediction["mean"], first_prediction["variance"])
```

Fitted GP models expose their [trained kernel](/references/python-api/models#openprotein.models.TrainedKernel), prior mean and observation noise variance. The mean uses the trained property units; noise uses those units squared. Hyperparameters are unavailable for GPs trained before they were recorded. The compatibility predictor also does not expose them for ensembles.

sections.heading: Criteria
sections.prose:
Build criteria from a trained model ID and a measurement name. A fitted `GPModel` from `session.models.GP` does not implement the comparison operators: construct `ModelCriterion` explicitly. The legacy `PredictorModel` supports comparisons for a single training property.

Use the authenticated `session` and the `assay` from the [Data upload example](/references/python-api/data). The GP trains on the assay's measured `activity` values. `fit.wait()` returns the fitted GP whose ID you pass to `ModelCriterion`:

```python
from openprotein.design import DesignConstraint, ModelCriterion, n_mutations

fit = session.models.GP().fit(assay=assay, property="activity")
gp = fit.wait(timeout=600)
low = (ModelCriterion(model_id=gp.id, measurement_name="activity") > 0.5) * 2.0
high = ModelCriterion(model_id=gp.id, measurement_name="activity") < 2.0
criteria = (low & high) | n_mutations(sequences=["ACDE"])

constraints = DesignConstraint("ACDE")
constraints.allow(amino_acids="GY", positions=[2])
design = session.design.create_genetic_algorithm_design(
    assay=assay, criteria=criteria, allowed_tokens=constraints
)
for result in design.wait(timeout=600):
    print(result.step, result.sample_index, result.sequence)
    print(result.scores, result.subscores, result.means, result.vars)
```

`*` sets a model criterion's weight, and comparisons set its target and direction; these operations modify the criterion. `&` joins subcriteria of the same type into a group, while `|` combines groups. Model and mutation-count subcriteria cannot be joined in the same `&` group. Constraints start with the original residues allowed; positions are 1-indexed and chain-break positions cannot be constrained.

sections.heading: Results
sections.prose: `get()` reads the results and `wait()` waits then reads; `stream(step=...)` can select a step. Each `DesignResult` carries `step`, `sample_index`, `sequence`, `scores`, `subscores`, `means` and `vars`. The SDK declares the last four as arrays but does not establish their scientific axes here; interpret them using the design and model context. Design result steps are 1-based. In `stream(step=...)`, use a 1-based step or `-1` for the last step.

Use `session.jobs.list(...)` and `session.jobs.get_job(...)` to inspect job records. Use `session.jobs.get(...)` to load the result reader. A job record describes the submission and its status; the reader provides methods to wait for and read results.

`wait_until_done()` waits for a terminal status and does not establish success: a failed or canceled job is also done. It does not fetch results. Check the job status before interpreting completion; result readers have their own failure and timeout behavior.

Given a stored job ID, refresh and check the status before reading results:

```python
from openprotein.errors import AuthError, JobFailedException, TimeoutException
from openprotein.jobs import JobStatus

try:
    future = session.jobs.get(job_id)
    future.wait_until_done(timeout=600)
    if future.status == JobStatus.SUCCESS:
        results = future.get()
    else:
        print("Job ended:", future.status, future.job.failure_message)
except TimeoutException as error:
    print("Polling timed out:", error)
except JobFailedException as error:
    print("Job failed:", error)
except AuthError as error:
    print("Authentication failed:", error)
```

`refresh()` updates the stored job record; `wait_until_done()` polls and updates it without reading results. The base `Future.get()` raises `JobFailedException` for `FAILURE`; some specialized readers have their own checks. `TimeoutException` covers polling timeouts. Network requests can also raise `requests.exceptions.Timeout`, an API `HTTPError`, or `openprotein.base.TimeoutError` for a gateway timeout. A timeout does not imply that the job was canceled.

`FutureUnit.get()` and `FutureUnit.wait()` raise `JobFailedException` when the unit is known to have failed or been canceled. A collection read can raise `JobOutputsNotReady` if the results are not ready; a direct position read can instead raise `HTTPError`. `InvalidJob` indicates a missing or invalid job.

sections.heading: Classes
sections.prose: [Future](#openprotein.jobs.Future) is the common job handle. `get()` and `wait()` read results according to the concrete future. For jobs that expose results by position, `Future` also provides named output selection and [per-position reads](#task-results).

sections.heading: Task job schemas
sections.prose: A [BatchJob](#openprotein.jobs.BatchJob) records the batch size in `num_records` when known. A [FutureUnit](#openprotein.jobs.FutureUnit) gives the position, status and error for one unit. Unit status uses the same [JobStatus](#openprotein.jobs.JobStatus) enum as job status.

sections.heading: Task results
sections.prose:
Use `job` from the [ESM2 embedding example](/references/python-api/models#interface) and choose a read based on what you need:

**Every position.** `wait()` waits for the job and reads its primary output, with one value per submitted position. Use `get()` if the job has already succeeded.

```python
embeddings = job.wait(timeout=600)
print(embeddings[0].shape)
```

**One position.** Use a zero-based position. `unit(0).wait()` waits for and reads just the first result. If that result is already available, use `get_item(0)`.

```python
embedding = job.unit(0).wait(timeout=600)
print(embedding.shape)
```

**One named output.** Check `job.outputs` for the names this job provides. Pass `output=` to select one by name. Different outputs can have different types. For this ESM2 job, `embeddings` is the primary output.

```python
print(job.outputs)
embeddings = job.wait(output="embeddings", timeout=600)
print(embeddings[0].shape)
```

See the [primary outputs and result types](/references/python-api/models#task-results) for other model tasks.

sections.heading: Fitted-model results
sections.prose: `SVDFitFuture`, `UMAPFitFuture` and `GPFitFuture` return the fitted model from bare `get()` and `wait()` calls. With `output=...`, these methods return values for the selected fit output. `CrossvalidateFuture` returns [`CrossvalidateResults`](#openprotein.jobs.CrossvalidateResults), parallel arrays with one row per sequence and measurement.

sections.heading: Job records and reloading
sections.prose: Model-task records use [Job](#openprotein.jobs.Job). Supported task records reload through `session.jobs.get(...)` as the corresponding task future. A reloaded job does not always retain the exact future class returned at submission: GP training uses [PredictorModel](/references/python-api/predictor#openprotein.predictor.PredictorModel), GP cross-validation uses [CVResultFuture](/references/python-api/predictor#openprotein.predictor.validate.CVResultFuture), and prompt sampling loads a stored [Prompt](/references/python-api/data#openprotein.data.Prompt). Refer to each reader's result contract.
Use `session.clustering` to access clustering.

sections.heading: Interface
sections.prose:
Choose either `sequences` or `assay`, not both. An assay can be an `AssayDataset`, `AssayMetadata` or assay ID. For an explicit sequence list the client checks a minimum of 2 and maximum of 10,000 sequences; this client-side list check does not inspect assay size.

Use a compatibility `EmbeddingModel` with a reduction for PLM features, or a compatibility `SVDModel` with `reduction=None` for SVD features. Those handles determine `feature_type`. When passing a model ID string instead, provide `feature_type="PLM"` or `"SVD"` explicitly; IDs are looked up through the corresponding compatibility API. PLM needs a reduction, SVD rejects one. `ward`, `centroid` and `median` linkage require `metric="euclidean"`.

Cluster the `assay` from the [Data upload example](/references/python-api/data):

```python
embedding_model = session.embedding.get_model("esm2_t33_650M_UR50D")
cluster_job = session.clustering.hierarchical(
    model=embedding_model, assay=assay, reduction="MEAN",
    linkage_method="ward", metric="euclidean",
)
result = cluster_job.wait(timeout=600)
print(result.n_leaves, result.leaf_order)
```

If you have sequences and no assay, pass the list directly:

```python
embedding_model = session.embedding.get_model("esm2_t33_650M_UR50D")
sequences = ["ACDEFGHIK", "ACDEYGHIK", "ACDEFGHLK"]
cluster_job = session.clustering.hierarchical(
    model=embedding_model, sequences=sequences, reduction="MEAN",
    linkage_method="ward", metric="euclidean",
)
result = cluster_job.wait(timeout=600)
print(result.linkage.shape, result.leaf_order)
```

Clustering accepts the compatibility handles above, not a `session.models` handle. Service availability and accepted combinations still depend on the selected model.

Use `session.align` to run alignments or build an MSA by homology search. If you already have an alignment file, use [`session.data.MSA.create()`](/references/python-api/data#openprotein.data.MSA.create) to upload it.

Create an alignment, inspect its first few rows, and attach it to a protein:

```python
from itertools import islice

from openprotein.molecules import Protein

sequence = "ACDEFGHIK"
msa = session.align.create_msa(sequence)
for name, aligned_sequence in islice(msa.wait(timeout=600), 3):
    print(name, aligned_sequence)

protein = Protein(sequence)
protein.msa = msa
```

`wait()` returns an iterator of `(name, aligned_sequence)` pairs. Attach the future `msa` itself; reading the rows is optional. `Protein.msa` also accepts a stored MSA handle or an ID. For a single-sequence model, `protein.msa = Protein.single_sequence_mode` explicitly selects no MSA; do not use that sentinel in place of an alignment for an MSA-requiring model. Model support varies.

For prompt sampling, `MSAFuture.sample_prompt` uses `num_sequences` and `num_residues`; [`MSA.sample_prompt`](/references/python-api/data#openprotein.data.MSA.sample_prompt) calls the corresponding limits `max_msa_sequences` and `max_msa_tokens`. Their defaults and validation differ.

Create prompts and queries for [PoET models](/references/python-api/models#openprotein.models.PoET). The Models interface accepts a prompt ID, a compatibility `Prompt`, or a stored Data `Prompt` as `prompt=` (or `None`). Use [`create_prompt()`](#openprotein.prompt.PromptAPI.create_prompt) to build a prompt from Python sequences, `Protein` objects, or `Complex` objects. To upload FASTA replicates or sample an alignment you already have, see [Data](/references/python-api/data#alignments-and-sampled-prompts).

```python
msa = session.align.create_msa("ACDEFGHIK")
prompt = msa.sample_prompt(num_sequences=10)
job = session.models.poet.embed(["ACDEFGHIK"], prompt=prompt)
```

Some pinned SDK docstrings still link to the deprecated embedding interface.

This compatibility interface is deprecated. Use [`session.models`](/references/python-api/models) for model access.

Create embeddings for your protein sequences using open-source and proprietary models! Note that for PoET Models, you will also need to supply a [`Prompt`](#openprotein.prompt.Prompt).

sections.heading: Models
sections.prose: These embedding models inherit from a base [`EmbeddingModel`](#openprotein.embeddings.EmbeddingModel), due to their shared functionality in providing the [`embed`](#openprotein.embeddings.EmbeddingModel.embed) method. These can also be used to fit the [`Transform Models`](#transform-models).

sections.heading: Transform Models
sections.prose:
These models are overlaid on top of the base embeddings models to produce reduced/transformed embeddings. [`SVDModel`](#openprotein.svd.SVDModel) represents an SVD model which is suitable to reduce the high-dimensional embeddings returned by base embedding models, whilst maintaining semantic information, fitted on your [`Assay`](#openprotein.data.Assay). You can fit your own SVD from any model's [`fit_svd`](#openprotein.embeddings.EmbeddingModel.fit_svd). [`UMAPModel`](#openprotein.umap.UMAPModel) represents a UMAP model which is suitable to project the high-dimensional embeddings into a lower dimension (usually 2) for visualization, to understand the semantic grouping within your [`Assay`](#openprotein.data.Assay). You can fit your own UMAP from any model's [`fit_umap`](#openprotein.embeddings.EmbeddingModel.fit_umap).

The legacy [`session.svd`](#openprotein.svd.SVDAPI) and [`session.umap`](#openprotein.umap.UMAPAPI) interfaces are deprecated compatibility APIs. For new code, create and manage these estimators through [`session.models.SVD`](/references/python-api/models#openprotein.models.ModelsAPI.SVD) and [`session.models.UMAP`](/references/python-api/models#openprotein.models.ModelsAPI.UMAP).
